subject: Critical Thinking
title: Slippery Slope: The Domino That Never Falls
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Slippery Slope: The Domino That Never Falls.

hook.text: 'Allow calculators in class and soon they'll forget math and civilization collapses!' Quite the leap in logic.

buildup.text: Slippery slope: arguing that one event will inevitably lead to a chain of increasingly extreme consequences.

discovery.text: The fallacy isn't claiming consequences exist – it's assuming each step inevitably follows without proving the causal.

twist.text: Sometimes slopes ARE slippery – addiction, authoritarianism, ecological collapse.

climax.text: Test each link: 'Does A really cause B? Does B really cause C?' If any link breaks, the slope doesn't slide.

punchline.text: Dominoes only fall if they're actually touching.

quiz.question: When is a slippery slope argument valid?
options: When each causal link in the chain is supported by evidence
When the final outcome is extreme enough

details.summary: A slippery slope argues that one small step will inevitably trigger a chain of increasingly extreme consequences. Without evidence linking each step, the argument exploits fear of catastrophe to block any change.
details.whyItMatters: Slippery slope arguments are used to resist any policy change by conjuring worst-case endpoints. Evaluating each link in the chain reveals whether the slope is real or imagined.
takeaways: The links between steps must be demonstrated, not assumed
Real causal chains exist but need evidence at each link
The argument works by emotional escalation, not logic

faq.question: Are all slippery slope arguments automatically fallacious?
faq.answer: No. If each step in the chain is supported by evidence, the argument may be valid. The fallacy occurs when the connections between steps are assumed without evidence, which is the case in most slippery slope claims.

faq.question: How do you evaluate whether a slippery slope argument has merit?
faq.answer: Examine each link in the chain independently. Is there evidence that step A leads to step B, and B to C? If any link is unsupported, the chain breaks and the slope is more imagined than real.
